title: Jason Barnwell — Agiloft (CLO, ex-Microsoft) on AI agents, declared protocols, and the rate of change in legal
pub: AI and the Future of Law podcast (AAA), hosts Jen Leonard & Bridget McCormack, YouTube
author: Jason Barnwell

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: The source shifts the emphasis from coordinated, lifelong competence reform toward enterprise resource constraints, machine-enabled value delivery and professional incentives as potentially faster drivers of change. It also argues that recruiting differently skilled students will achieve little if the underlying professional model remains unchanged.
qs: Those are the macro patterns I’m seeing that make me think the rate of change may not be predicated on somebody learning this in school, surviving the tournament, and eventually getting enough power to institutionalize it decades from now.
But how frustrated would one of those people be if they were selected and then plugged into a model that hasn’t changed at all?

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The excerpt provides only host-supplied background and framing before Barnwell answers. It contains no substantive Barnwell claim about practitioner-led experimentation, redesign, implementation, reliability, access to justice, judicial legitimacy or governance, so his position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Barnwell accepts that automation changes traditional junior work and materially extends the cluster’s proposed response by advocating declared protocols, synthetic matter simulations and high-variety experimentation to accelerate learning. These are concrete training mechanisms, though presented as hypotheses rather than validated substitutes for supervised live practice.
qs: The rate of learning for me was fundamentally constrained by whatever client work came in that was suitable for me to do.

One of the things that could be different now—and it might be a very different way of training people into our practice and our profession—is that we start running them through simulations of deals, disputes, regulatory inquiries, whatever it might be.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Barnwell accepts the cluster’s core view that AI value requires changing legal production rather than merely improving existing tasks. He materially extends it by identifying culture and incentives as the mechanism obstructing institutional absorption and by urging lawyers to design new forms of value instead of preserving established processes. His claims are conceptual and predictive rather than empirically demonstrated.
qs: And there are two things that shape human behavior at scale: culture and incentives.
Your highest and best purpose is to go build new cranks—to really take the lid off the value function of what we can provide.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI changes legal-service production more than it eliminates lawyers, then materially extends it by urging the profession to move beyond accelerating familiar tasks and develop broader forms of business and client value. It also stresses lawyers’ role in shaping that redesign.
qs: It’s really hard to get lawyers to move away from, “This will help me draft a lease faster,” or, “This will help me summarize a court filing faster,” toward the bigger, bolder experiments you’re talking about—the ones that actually let you get ahead in your business and in the service you provide to clients.
I want the legal profession in the game when it comes to figuring out what the future looks like, because law is still the operating system of our society.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Barnwell accepts the cluster’s framing of legal AI as service and organisational redesign rather than mere task acceleration. He materially extends it by identifying culture and incentives as behavioural mechanisms and proposing that lawyers codify tacit expertise into explicit instructions, taxonomies and protocols that support scalable, human-controlled AI workflows. He presents these mechanisms as hypotheses and early experimentation, not demonstrated transformation.
qs: And there are two things that shape human behavior at scale: culture and incentives.

One of my hypotheses is that the people who are going to get the most value out of these emerging experiences are the people who can engage in the metacognitive process of cracking open the heuristics they’ve earned over time and effectively decompiling them into explicit instructions that can be handed off to one of these magic boxes.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Barnwell supports redesigning legal delivery beyond isolated task acceleration. He argues that professional culture and incentives entrench established workflows and urges lawyers to create new forms of value as technology absorbs repetitive work. His contribution is directional and anecdotal, without addressing the cluster’s broader pricing, verification, staffing or market evidence claims.
qs: And there are two things that shape human behavior at scale: culture and incentives.
Your highest and best purpose is to go build new cranks—to really take the lid off the value function of what we can provide.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: Barnwell’s account supports the synthesis’s cautious distinction between promising agentic workflows and autonomous, production-ready practice. His experiments show conversational skill-building and repeatable playbooks, but he characterises the skills as rudimentary and stresses deliberate, sandboxed deployment; he does not address whether specialist legal vendors will be displaced.
qs: Of course, it’s really cool, but it’s also not really a product, so you need to be very intentional about how you deploy it.
It basically creates its own playbook, and that’s how it starts to generate fairly rudimentary, repeatable skills.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Barnwell supports the cluster’s core view that AI will redesign and augment legal work rather than eliminate its underlying complexity. His Agiloft example illustrates a substantial gain on a specific analytical workflow, while his qualification about difficult compliance problems is consistent with jagged capability and selective deployment. His agentic and market-acceleration claims are forward-looking rather than evidence of general autonomy or realised sector-wide value.
qs: That was something that would have been incredibly hard a few years ago—now it’s Bennett doing a thing on a Wednesday in half an hour.

I talk to friends and colleagues practicing in other places, and they’re like, “Man, I’ve got this EU Data Act issue and I’m not sure how I’m going to drive compliance.” And I’m thinking to myself: those things are still hard, because the world is complex.

kp.k: Agentic prototyping lowers barriers but creates coordination risks
kp.d: Barnwell describes using OpenClaw through Telegram to develop repeatable skills documented in markdown, then using Claude Code to deploy an application in about 15 minutes. The scheduling application subsequently sent his wife hundreds of invitations, illustrating his distinction between controlled personal tools and systems affecting others. This personal experiment, not a systematic test, underpins his warning that cheap creation can generate excessive demands and interruptions without testing and governance.
qs: It basically creates its own playbook, and that’s how it starts to generate fairly rudimentary, repeatable skills.
It was a little more complicated than that, but I had it go live in about 15 minutes.
It hadn’t gone through all the user-acceptance testing you’d want.
It’s going to be very easy to create punitive levels of engagement, asks, and interruptions at every layer.

kp.k: Constrained permissions accompany experimental agent deployment
kp.d: Barnwell reports sandboxing OpenClaw on a $10-a-month virtual private server, separating permissions and giving it its own M365 identity rather than his account. It could see his free-busy availability but could not change his calendar. These are the safeguards in his personal setup, not evidence of a validated legal deployment standard.
qs: I provisioned a virtual private server, sandboxed it, segmented permissions, and did all the things.
So I got a $10-a-month virtual private server running somewhere in Oregon.
I’ve given it constrained access. It can see my free-busy availability, but it can’t change my calendar.

kp.k: Tool-making capabilities may compound rather than incrementally improve
kp.d: From experimenting with different models, Barnwell observes that more tool-capable models can decompose problems and fashion intermediate tools. He hypothesizes divergent benefits: some users obtain incremental improvements to existing tasks, while others achieve potentially exponential gains by treating tools as means to create further tools. He explicitly remains uncertain about how to foster the latter disposition.
qs: As you use a model that’s more tool-capable, it can solve harder problems, because it can break what you’re trying to do into smaller intermediate steps and fashion its own tools to get through them.
Tools can make better tools, which can make better tools.
I’m not sure how to get people to opt into that second view of the world.

kp.k: Professional incentives favor repetition over redesign
kp.d: Barnwell explicitly generalizes that legal culture rewards intensive execution of known methods, making successful practitioners difficult to redirect toward building new ways of delivering value. Leonard and McCormack separately report that expansive experimentation is unusual in the legal audiences they encounter. Barnwell frames automation as challenging a scarcity-based professional model, rather than providing measured evidence of displacement.
qs: And there are two things that shape human behavior at scale: culture and incentives.
our profession tends to select for, recognize, reward, and promote people who are really good at grinding.
the crank you used to turn can now be turned by something else.
Your highest and best purpose is to go build new cranks—to really take the lid off the value function of what we can provide.

kp.k: Buyer substitution could accelerate otherwise generational change
kp.d: Barnwell contrasts a slow-change scenario, in which innovators must accumulate power under incumbents before institutionalizing new methods, with his preferred expectation of faster commercial change. He argues that falling capability-access barriers intensify competition and that legal buyers' willingness to change purchasing habits and entertain substitutes determines the pace. His expectation of rapidly unlocked demand is conditional on such changes becoming socially acceptable, with no quantified timeline.
qs: So the bear case here is: does this take a generation?
I don’t think so.
how fast are buyers of legal services willing to change their buying habits, and what kinds of substitutes are they willing to entertain?
Once it becomes tasteful to make those changes, I think a lot of demand gets unlocked very quickly.

kp.k: In-house resource allocation increasingly requires demonstrated business value
kp.d: Speaking from his enterprise role, Barnwell says a constrained resource envelope and expectations of returns to capital push legal toward machine-enabled delivery. Incremental resources increasingly require a data-informed value case based on speed, scale, or control, including governance and compliance, rather than assurances that legal is managing risk. This is a practitioner account of resource allocation, not a measured industry-wide finding.
qs: My CFO is effectively saying, “Here is your envelope of resources.”
But increasingly, any incremental resource in the enterprise is gated on a data-informed story about value delivery.
Does it create speed? Does it create scale? Does it create control—meaning governance or compliance?

kp.k: Alternative careers may change professional status and recruitment
kp.d: Barnwell sees academic incentives as poorly aligned with the emerging value model and proposes that visible success in alternative careers could attract status and institutional attention. Leonard reports alumni moving to Harvey and other legal-tech startups; McCormack reports strong applicants for newly emerging legal-engineering crossover roles at her organization. These are distinct speakers' observations and hypotheses, not representative hiring data.
qs: the incentive models for the academics who really do control law schools feel very far away from the things we’re talking about.
But if that alternative path starts producing visible success, status, and relevance, institutions will take more notice, because they do want to remain relevant.
Now I’m seeing my alums go to Harvey and to really interesting legal tech startups.
we now have needs for these crossover roles—roles we’re almost making up names for—that sit between legal and engineering.

kp.k: Structured contract data supports faster portfolio analysis
kp.d: Barnwell describes CLM spanning bargaining, documentation, performance and enforcement, and claims that embedded AI benefits from its structured context. As an internal example, he says his legal operations head used Agiloft to identify customers whose negotiated agreements might require engagement about a proposed change, in half an hour on the preceding Wednesday. This is a vendor executive's anecdote and accuracy claim, without independent validation or reported accuracy measures.
qs: rather than bolting AI on as an afterthought, we have AI experiences that take advantage of the rich information already inside our system.
So you get higher accuracy and better results.
he used Agiloft to run that question across our customer base and identify which customers might have thoughts and feelings about this, and we should think about engaging them on this topic.
That was something that would have been incredibly hard a few years ago—now it’s Bennett doing a thing on a Wednesday in half an hour.

kp.k: Parallel agents reposition lawyers as work architects
kp.d: Barnwell describes forthcoming agentic capabilities and parallel work as opportunities to increase scale and precision. He predicts a shift toward humans defining objectives, constraints, context and desired outcomes for delegated tasks, analogous to managing associates. The claim concerns changed orchestration skills and machine-enabled capacity, not a quantified change in associate-to-partner ratios.
qs: we’re about to start lighting up agentic capabilities
Because what that really does is reposition the human. You really do become the architect.

What you’re trying to do is create the conditions for these parallel efforts to deliver outcomes that align with the objective, operate within the constraints, and match the value function you define.
It’s a little like what we used to do when we managed associates.

kp.k: Explicit expertise becomes more valuable than guarded heuristics
kp.d: Barnwell hypothesizes that practitioners who can translate tacit expertise into explicit machine instructions will gain the most from emerging tools. He contrasts this with scarcity-based rewards for possessing undisclosed knowledge and recommends converting known work into declared protocols. McCormack additionally identifies knowledge transfer to new professionals as a benefit.
qs: One of my hypotheses is that the people who are going to get the most value out of these emerging experiences are the people who can engage in the metacognitive process of cracking open the heuristics they’ve earned over time and effectively decompiling them into explicit instructions that can be handed off to one of these magic boxes.
In the past, not doing that benefited you, because you had the secret.
we need to turn our known work—the work where we know the type of it and we know what to do with it—into declared protocols.

kp.k: Simulations could decouple lawyer training from incoming client work
kp.d: Barnwell contrasts his early learning, constrained by suitable client matters, with a proposed model of AI-generated deals, disputes and regulatory inquiries offering near-real-time feedback on choices and trade-offs. Documented organization-specific protocols could strengthen this training. McCormack endorses simulation by analogy with other professions, while Leonard describes faster learning in a varied, psychologically safe municipal practice. The discussion offers a training proposal and personal experience, not evaluated educational outcomes.
qs: The rate of learning for me was fundamentally constrained by whatever client work came in that was suitable for me to do.
These tools can generate synthetic scenarios trained on the kinds of things that happen in the real world.
Then they can give people feedback in near real time: you chose to do this, here are other options you could have considered, here are the trade-offs.
Giving people the ability to experiment in a high-variety environment is one of the fastest ways to learn.

kp.k: Layered knowledge architectures could address playbook coverage gaps
kp.d: Barnwell values conventional playbooks but argues that they cover only previously encountered, documented situations, while variation may grow in breadth and volume. He describes an early internal experiment linking organizational strategy and constitutional values to policies and protocols. He hypothesizes that taxonomy and ontology could help machines identify gaps and suggest responses from higher-level guidance and neighboring protocols, while giving humans a scalable management structure. He stresses the experiment's preliminary status and retains human contextualization and refinement.
qs: The challenge is that you only have coverage on the things you’ve already seen and had time to reduce to practice and document.
This is literally an experiment we’re starting to run internally, so this is the wettest of paint.
And if something comes in and hits one of your void spaces at the protocol level, maybe you can at least have a starting theory of how to think about it based on the layers stacked above.
it may be the case that the machines become very useful in identifying the gaps you have and suggesting a starting theory for what belongs there.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Barnwell predicts divergent benefits from AI: incremental improvements for conventional users versus compounding gains for people who use tools to build further tools.
pts.d: Jason Barnwell describes tool-capable models as able to decompose harder problems and create intermediate tools. He explicitly labels the projected divergence between user groups a hypothesis. Applied to legal practice, he argues that established, repetitive value-producing work can increasingly be performed by machines, shifting lawyers' highest-value contribution toward designing new ways to deliver services.

pts.k: Barnwell predicts that cheaper AI-enabled creation can generate excessive demands on others unless deployment is governed.
pts.d: He distinguishes a tool operating for one user from systems interacting with other people and machines. He extrapolates from a personal scheduling-agent failure to institutional and societal risks: lower production costs can create excessive requests and interruptions. This is a general deployment claim relevant to legal institutions, not a demonstrated legal-services outcome.

pts.k: Barnwell expects legal-market change to depend more on buyers accepting substitutes and enterprise resource pressures than on generational turnover.
pts.d: He presents entrenched culture and incentives as barriers, but does not expect change necessarily to require a generation. Falling barriers to AI capabilities can change competition quickly, especially in private commercial legal services. He predicts rapid demand shifts once changing purchasing practices becomes acceptable. He also argues that resource-constrained legal departments increasingly need machine-enabled capacity and data-informed accounts of speed, scale, and governance to obtain additional resources. His reference to machine leverage concerns technology-enabled capacity, not associate-to-partner staffing leverage.

pts.k: Barnwell proposes alternative career success as a possible mechanism for changing legal education and professional incentives.
pts.d: He suggests that some people who would otherwise follow conventional legal careers may instead solve problems through alternative paths. A smaller group achieving visible success could acquire status and induce institutions to adapt. These are possibilities, not reported labour-market findings. The hosts' examples of moves to Harvey and hiring for legal-engineering roles are not Barnwell's evidence or claims.

pts.k: Barnwell claims embedded AI makes contract information more usable and sharply reduces the effort required for portfolio-wide analysis.
pts.d: Speaking as Agiloft's CLO, he says its embedded AI benefits from existing structured contract context, producing higher accuracy and better results. He reports that his head of legal operations used Agiloft to identify customers whose agreements might require engagement over a proposed change in approximately half an hour. He contrasts this with labour-intensive manual review earlier in his career. This is an internal use example and a product-performance assertion, not a quantified accuracy evaluation.

pts.k: Barnwell predicts parallel agentic work will increase capacity and shift lawyers toward designing and directing workflows.
pts.d: He announces forthcoming Agiloft agentic capabilities and expects greater scale and precision from parallel execution. Humans become architects who define objectives, constraints, and desired outcomes, analogous to directing associates. He hypothesises that lawyers who can convert tacit expertise into explicit instructions will gain the most value, reversing the historical advantage of keeping specialised know-how private. This describes delegated execution with human direction, not an explicit claim that legal work can be relied on without human oversight.

pts.k: Barnwell predicts declared protocols and AI-generated simulations could accelerate training and reduce dependence on available client work.
pts.d: He proposes documenting known work as explicit protocols to transfer knowledge to incoming team members. Synthetic deals, disputes, and regulatory inquiries could provide varied practice and near-real-time feedback on options and trade-offs. Context-specific protocols would further strengthen this approach. He contrasts the proposal with his own early learning, which depended on suitable client matters arriving, and suggests high-variety experimentation may be more valuable in a dynamic environment than narrowly refining familiar tasks.

pts.k: Barnwell hypothesises that structured organisational knowledge can help machines identify gaps in legal playbooks and suggest responses while preserving human control.
pts.d: He expects growing breadth and volume of unfamiliar situations to expose gaps in existing playbooks. His proposed architecture connects organisational purpose and values to policies and protocols, supported by taxonomy and ontology. Machines could use these layers and neighbouring protocols to suggest initial approaches where no protocol exists; humans would contextualise and refine them. He describes this as a newly starting internal experiment rather than an established result.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Barnwell's evidence consists principally of personal experiments, internal operational examples, professional experience, and explicitly speculative reasoning.
pts.d: For agent capability and deployment risk, he reports building a scheduling application through Claude Code and OpenClaw in about 15 minutes, followed by unintended mass invitations; he also describes sandboxing, constrained permissions, and trying different models. For contract analytics, he offers the approximately half-hour internal customer-contract exercise, without reporting portfolio size, accuracy measurements, or independent validation. Market-change arguments draw on his experience with enterprise resource allocation and observations about professional incentives; an unnamed business-school article supplies an analogy about institutional change. Training proposals draw on his early-career experience and discussions about simulations. The information-architecture proposal is an early internal experiment. No systematic labour-market data, legal-task benchmarks, or measured training outcomes are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source combines present capabilities and recent anecdotes with imminent product plans and undated, conditional predictions.
pts.d: In the supplied 2026 transcript, the OpenClaw experiments occurred a few weeks earlier, the contract-analysis example occurred the previous day, and Agiloft's embedded-AI investments span the preceding couple of years. Agentic features are described as about to launch, without a date. Barnwell rejects generational delay as his expected scenario but gives no numerical adoption forecast: buyer willingness, acceptable substitutes, declining access barriers, and resource incentives determine the pace. Compounding benefits depend on exploratory tool use; effective delegation depends on explicit expertise and well-defined constraints. Simulation training and knowledge-architecture benefits remain prospective and conditional. He acknowledges that software testing remains difficult and that legal compliance problems remain complex.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are commercial legal buyers, in-house teams, practising lawyers, trainees, legal education institutions, and CLM customers.
pts.d: Private commercial buyers can accelerate market change by changing purchasing habits and considering substitutes. Resource-constrained corporate legal departments and legal operations teams can gain analytical capacity but face stronger expectations to demonstrate value. Lawyers doing repeatable work face a shift toward workflow design, explicit instruction, and supervision of parallel efforts; those able to externalise expertise are predicted to benefit most. New team members and trainees could gain faster knowledge transfer and more varied practice through protocols and simulations. Law schools and professional institutions may face pressure from successful alternative career paths. Agiloft is discussed as a software vendor serving contract-management customers, not as an alternative legal service provider. Families, institutions, and society appear in the broader warning about automated demands; Barnwell does not offer a specific access-to-justice or lawyer-headcount forecast.
